verdict: Lend in Sri City electronics at the data call of OK, but only to component and enclosure suppliers with real volume and short cycles; treat memory-driven revenue inflation and thin-margin assemblers as Caution.
title: Sri City Electronics Manufacturing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**An electronics unit here buys components, chips and enclosures, runs SMT lines and assembly, and sells finished boards or boxes to an OEM on 30-90 day terms.** Cash sits in inventory (chips, imported parts) and receivables, not in the plant; the line itself is modest capex, the working-capital cycle is the loan. Pricing power is thin because the OEM sets the price, so margin comes from utilisation and component buying. **When a proposal lands, check the inventory days and the customer concentration first; if one buyer is above half of sales, ask for the purchase order and the payment history with that buyer.**

## What has changed now
**National electronics output is up 19.3% YoY and 13.6% Apr-to-date [D], and electronics exports are up 44.0% Apr-to-date in USD [D], so volumes are genuinely moving.** Andhra Pradesh electricity demand is up 18.1% Apr-to-date against India's 9.5% [D], which tells us local plants are running. But peer results show the catch: Dixon's revenue rose 47% to Rs.21,794 crore while margins compressed and working capital rose [6][7], and part of that revenue is memory-chip price inflation, not more units [4]. **So when a proposal shows 40%-plus revenue growth, ask how much is price and how much is volume; if it is price, size the loan on units, not on the inflated turnover.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue the tier-2 suppliers feeding the Sri City cluster: enclosure and sheet-metal makers, PCB assembly job-workers, cable and harness units, and packaging suppliers to the anchor OEMs.** These have shorter cycles, local customers and less chip exposure. The rating file on DEAPL shows what a good electronics supplier looks like: revenue growth of 388% in FY2025 and 182% in H1 FY2026 with RoCE of 50% and above [10]. **Avoid pure assemblers whose entire margin is a conversion fee and whose buyer dictates component prices; if the buyer names the component vendor, ask who bears the inventory.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure each limit around the working-capital cycle, not the plant: cash credit against stock and receivables with a drawing power recalculated monthly, and a term loan only for the SMT line with a moratorium matched to customer ramp.** Take stock and receivable statements every month, plus the top-five buyer ledger and the electricity bill. **If receivables days cross the stated cycle by more than the agreed buffer, cut drawing power immediately and ask for the buyer's payment confirmation.** Local project news for Sri City itself is thin in these sources [1][2], so lean on first principles and the peer numbers above.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch inventory build against flat offtake, a single buyer stretching terms, and any shift from own-brand to pure job-work.** Dixon's margin compression alongside revenue growth [6] is the pattern to fear. **If a borrower's stock rises while dispatches fall for two months, treat it as a demand problem and re-rate the limit.**
watch: Receivable days exceed agreed cycle by buffer -> cut drawing power and seek buyer confirmation
Monthly electricity bill and dispatch register
Dispatches fall two months while stock rises -> re-rate limit, ask for order book
Top buyer above half of sales -> seek diversification plan or reduce exposure
Monthly component price index for memory
Input price rise with flat units -> size loan on units, not turnover
